item.title: Two charged with murder over death of Vimal Nand
item.description: Two men have been charged with murder following the death of 38-year-old Vimal Nand after an alleged assault in Sigatoka over the weekend. Police confirmed the two accused, aged 19 and 51, will be produced at the Sigatoka Magistrates Court on Thursday, August 13.
item.content:encoded:
Two men have been charged with murder following the death of 38-year-old Vimal Nand after an alleged assault in Sigatoka over the weekend.

Police confirmed the two accused, aged 19 and 51, will be produced at the Sigatoka Magistrates Court on Thursday, August 13.

The pair have been jointly charged with one count of murder, one count of act with intent to cause grievous harm and one count of assault causing actual bodily harm.

The charges follow an alleged confrontation involving Nand, his son and another student while they were out horse riding.

According to police, the two suspects allegedly confronted the three over the weekend.

Nand was later found unconscious by his brother with serious head injuries.

He was initially taken to Sigatoka Hospital before being transferred to Nadi Hospital and subsequently to Lautoka Hospital because of the seriousness of his injuries.

Nand later died at Lautoka Hospital despite attempts to revive him.

The two accused are expected to make their first court appearance on the charges at the Sigatoka Magistrates Court on Thursday.

item.title: Classify security services as essential, says Nand
item.description: SECURITY services must be formally classified as an essential service alongside the police force to ensure guards receive proper professional recognition and resources, says Professional Security Services regional manager West Sanjay Kumar Nand. Making the plea during the public consultation on the review of the Security Industry Act 2010 yesterday, Mr Nand said that private guards were consistent
item.content:encoded:
SECURITY services must be formally classified as an essential service alongside the police force to ensure guards receive proper professional recognition and resources, says Professional Security Services regional manager West Sanjay Kumar Nand.

Making the plea during the public consultation on the review of the Security Industry Act 2010 yesterday, Mr Nand said that private guards were consistently on the front lines during major crises.

“COVID is there, natural disasters is there, everything is there. Our guards are still at the sites. We are still in the field,” he said.

During strict movement curfews, Mr Nand said officers were required to remain active round-the-clock to check on personnel, monitor client properties, and protect closed premises from looting.

“I think the industry should be an essential service permanently.

“So that we will get the recognition we deserve. And, at the same time, we will also get the perks which come along with it, like the training aspect.”

Mr Nand said many commercial clients failed to prioritise security until after a severe incident occurred.

He said property owners frequently relied on basic measures such as lighting and surveillance equipment, which failed to deter intruders who concealed their identities.

“Thieves nowadays cover themselves from head to toe.

“They look at the camera, they wave at the camera, they break things, they take stuff out, they move and they know they can’t be detected because there is no clue.”

item.title: Calls for major reforms
item.description: Fiji’s private security industry is calling for major reforms to the Security Industry Act 2010, with concerns over worker exploitation, high staff turnover and changing workforce dynamics prompting calls for a modern regulatory framework. The concerns were raised during a public consultation on the review of the Act at the Sugar Cane Growers Council boardroom in Lautoka yesterday.
item.content:encoded:
Fiji’s private security industry is calling for major reforms to the Security Industry Act 2010, with concerns over worker exploitation, high staff turnover and changing workforce dynamics prompting calls for a modern regulatory framework.

The concerns were raised during a public consultation on the review of the Act at the Sugar Cane Growers Council boardroom in Lautoka yesterday.

Professional Security Services regional manager West Sanjay Kumar Nand said stronger regulation was needed to protect security guards and improve standards across the industry.

He said some non-compliant employers continued to exploit workers by failing to provide basic employment benefits.

“In terms of rights, many of their guards have come running to us,” Mr Nand said.

“They don’t give them FNPF or any leave. Sometimes they even exploit their workers, paying them only partially.”

He said poor working conditions had contributed to high staff turnover, making it increasingly difficult for companies to retain experienced guards.

“We are always looking for guards. This is an industry where the turnover is very high. People just come, and as soon as they get something better, they go.”

Mr Nand also noted a decline in former military and police personnel entering the sector, with more attractive career opportunities drawing experienced workers elsewhere.

The review of the 2010 Act is expected to strengthen industry regulation, improve worker protections and ensure the sector keeps pace with changing workforce needs.

ESCALATING on-the-job risks have sparked urgent calls to allow private security guards to carry batons and handcuffs, following public consultations yesterday on the review of the Security Industry Act 2010 in Lautoka.

Speaking after session proceedings at the Sugar Cane Growers Council boardroom, Commissioner for the review of the Act Ana Rokomokoti emphasised that evolving workplace dangers necessitate stronger protective measures for frontline personnel.

“The idea is to give them an opportunity to be able to defend themselves, considering that the security environment nowadays is very different from what it was ten years ago,” she said.

“The risks are higher and there’s more exposure to such risks.”

Ms Rokomokoti said that 16 years have passed since the original legislation was enacted, making the current review critical to addressing modern operational realities but she stressed that updating the legal framework required direct feedback from those working within the industry.

“A lot has changed in the security landscape, and this review is very timely, but the review cannot be successful without the input from the members of the public.

“I’d really plead with especially those who are involved in the security business to come forward and give us their views.” Professional Security Services Ltd regional manager West Sanjay Kumar Nand pointed out that the lack of restraint equipment posed severe safety hazards for officers handling volatile individuals

A VAST majority of security company employees and employers are calling for the implementing of 12-hour shifts particularly for those looking to make more income for their families.

This was highlighted during a public consultation on the review of the Security Act 2010 held at the Sugar Cane Growers Council boardroom in Lautoka yesterday.

Speaking at the public consultation on the review of the Security Industry Act 2010,

Commissioner for Ana Rokomokoti said this was also highlighted during the initial consultation in Suva on Monday.

“There was a good turnout in Suva, there was a lot of emphasis on the shift, from 8 hours to 12 hours but of course, I accept that the propositions coming from employer’s perspective,” she said.

“There is a suggestion that the 12-hour shift is something that the government should consider shifting towards and they gave the pros and cons.”

Ms Rokomokoti said many employees were focused on the take homer salary at the end of the week, particularly for security guards who were also sole breadwinners for their families.

“I think we had the figures from $227 or $220 to $331 per week net (if approved ).” Ms Rokomokoti said this suggestion seemed to be one agreed upon by both employers and employees, but the committee would also need to sort through the written submissions made via email.

item.title: Catholic Church celebrates 184 years
item.description: LAKEBA Island in Lau will become the centre of celebrations this weekend, marking 184 years of Catholic faith in Fiji. The celebrations, beginning on Friday and concluding on Sunday, will commemorate the arrival of Catholicism in Fiji in 1842 — two years before the first Catholic missionaries officially arrived in the country in 1844.
item.content:encoded:
LAKEBA Island in Lau will become the centre of celebrations this weekend, marking 184 years of Catholic faith in Fiji.

The celebrations, beginning on Friday and concluding on Sunday, will commemorate the arrival of Catholicism in Fiji in 1842 — two years before the first Catholic missionaries officially arrived in the country in 1844.

Archbishop Peter Loy Chong said Lakeba was chosen because of its significant place in the history of the Catholic Church in Fiji. He said Catholicism was first introduced to Fiji by catechist Mosese Vaitaba, who was left on Lakeba by missionaries and arrived two years before the missionaries themselves.

“So this year is quite a memorable one for Catholics and Christians as a whole in Fiji,” Archbishop Loy Chong said.

He said the anniversary provided an opportunity for the church to reflect on its past, assess its present position and consider its future.

The celebrations will be kept low-key and focused on the Lakeba community, following the recent installation of the Tui Nayau, which placed significant demands on the island’s resources.

Rather than bringing large numbers from Viti Levu and elsewhere, the church has sent a small team comprising a priest, seminarian and two catechists to support local celebrations and renew understanding of the faith.

A plaque and stage commemorating the arrival of Catholicism will also be blessed.

Archbishop Loy Chong said the anniversary was not simply about history, but about renewing faith for future generations.

item.title: Bulou champions youth and women
item.description: AT just four years old, Bulou Boteiova experienced a loss that would shape much of her life — the death of her father. Growing up with grief at such a young age was difficult, but through the years, her mother became her strongest source of strength, carrying the responsibilities of both parents and guiding her through the challenges of growing up without her father.
item.content:encoded:
AT just four years old, Bulou Boteiova experienced a loss that would shape much of her life — the death of her father.

Growing up with grief at such a young age was difficult, but through the years, her mother became her strongest source of strength, carrying the responsibilities of both parents and guiding her through the challenges of growing up without her father.

For Ms Bulou, 23, the experience has taught her the value of family, faith and community, and the importance of having people to lean on during life’s hardest moments.

“I am so thankful to God that my mum, who is a prayer warrior, plays both roles as a mother and a father,” she reflects.

The 2024 Miss Coral Coast Queen is competing in this year’s Hibiscus Festival with a purpose that reaches beyond the crown. She is using the platform to champion youth and women’s empowerment, determined to speak for those whose voices are often overlooked.

“In that way, I can give back to the community.”

Ms Bulou believes young people have the power to make positive decisions about their lives when they are given the right skills, opportunities and resources.

Originally from Teci Village in the Yasawa Group, with maternal ties to Marou Village in the district of Naviti, Yasawa, Ms Bulou was raised in Uciwai Settlement in Korolevu, Baravi, Nadroga.

Today, she serves her community as a Year 6 teacher.

Her journey has also been inspired by one woman she greatly admires — Lenora Qereqeretabua — whose presence and advocacy have influenced Ms Bulou’s own aspirations.

“One day, I want to be like her, fighting for the rights of the people in our country.”

item.title: Cabinet endorses changes to Electoral Act
item.description: Cabinet has endorsed a series of proposed amendments to the Electoral Act 2014 aimed at making Fiji’s electoral system more inclusive, accessible and transparent. The proposed amendments seek to remove requirements that may unnecessarily prevent eligible voters from participating in elections while also introducing changes designed to improve access to voting.
item.content:encoded:
Cabinet has endorsed a series of proposed amendments to the Electoral Act 2014 aimed at making Fiji’s electoral system more inclusive, accessible and transparent.

The proposed amendments seek to remove requirements that may unnecessarily prevent eligible voters from participating in elections while also introducing changes designed to improve access to voting.

-Removal of unnecessary voting requirements

-Improved accessibility for persons with disabilities.

-Stronger electoral quality assurance measures

-Greater clarity around electoral procedures.

-Measures to create a more level playing field for political parties

-Clearer rules for referendum campaigning

The proposed changes form part of efforts to strengthen Fiji’s electoral framework and address barriers that could affect voter participation.

A significant focus is on accessibility, with the proposed expansion of postal voting and measures for persons with disabilities intended to provide more opportunities for eligible voters to participate.

Changes to the ballot paper are also proposed, with the new format intended to make candidate and political party identification clearer for voters at polling stations.

The proposed amendments will also address the regulatory environment surrounding political parties and referendum campaigns.

Cabinet said the overall objective is to ensure Fiji’s electoral processes remain accessible, transparent and clear for voters.

item.title: Police continue probe into two FICAC officers linked to Charlie Charters case
item.description: POLICE have confirmed that investigations into two former Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption (FICAC) officers linked to the alleged disclosure of confidential internal FICAC information to Charlie Charters are continuing. Assistant Commissioner of Police Crime Loraini Seru told The Fiji Times : “The investigation into the other two continues.”
item.content:encoded:
POLICE have confirmed that investigations into two former Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption (FICAC) officers linked to the alleged disclosure of confidential internal FICAC information to Charlie Charters are continuing.

Assistant Commissioner of Police Crime Loraini Seru told The Fiji Times : “The investigation into the other two continues.”

The matter was referred to Police by FICAC under section 13F of the FICAC Act following allegations concerning the disclosure of official information.

On June 30, FICAC said any decision on whether former FICAC officers would face charges would rest with Police.

The update comes after the High Court permanently stayed the criminal proceedings against citizen journalist Charlie Charters.

In its ruling, the High Court stayed the charges against Mr Charters because of issues relating to the State’s case and FICAC’s conduct in bringing the proceedings.

The two FICAC officers in question were accused of divulging internal information to Mr Charters without written authorisation, violating Section 13G (1) of the FICAC Act.

Police did not provide further details, with no charges announced at this stage.

item.description: THE two sureties for a man accused of attempted murder have been ordered to appear before the High Court after he failed to attend court as required under his bail conditions. Prosecutor Hezekiah Nofaga informed Justice Dane Tuiqereqere that Saimoni Rokotunidau, who is charged with the attempted murder of Police Constable Senoveva Tikoduadua, remained at large and had also sold the property where
item.content:encoded:
THE two sureties for a man accused of attempted murder have been ordered to appear before the High Court after he failed to attend court as required under his bail conditions.

Prosecutor Hezekiah Nofaga informed Justice Dane Tuiqereqere that Saimoni Rokotunidau, who is charged with the attempted murder of Police Constable Senoveva Tikoduadua, remained at large and had also sold the property where he had been residing.

The State applied for the sureties to be summoned to explain Mr Rokotunidau’s non-attendance.

Justice Tuiqereqere granted the application and directed the two sureties to appear on August 25.

Mr Rokotunidau is charged in relation to an incident in April in which Constable Tikoduadua was allegedly struck by a vehicle while manning a police checkpoint in Laqere, Nasinu.

The police officer is the daughter of Defence and Veterans Affairs Minister Pio Tikoduadua.

Mr Rokotunidau also faces a count each of unlawful possession of illicit drugs, going equipped for theft, serious assault, and refusing to have his fingerprints and photographs taken.
